title: Lessons from 15 Months of Building LLM Agents
summary: What we learned shipping autonomous coding agents to hundreds of engineering teams. Sandboxing, context management, cost control, and the things that actually matter.
body_text: We have been building production LLM agents since late 2023. In that time, we have shipped agents that review code, generate pull requests, fix bugs, answer questions about codebases, write reports, and run analytics queries. They run autonomously, 24/7, across hundreds of repositories. Here is what we have learned. None of this is theoretical — these are lessons from production systems handling real workloads. Sandboxing is non-negotiable An autonomous coding agent needs to execute code. It needs to run tests, install dependencies, invoke build tools. If you give it access to your production environment, you are one hallucinated rm -rf away from an incident. Every agent invocation in Ellipsis runs in an isolated sandbox — a fresh container with a cloned copy of the repository, network access restricted to approved endpoints, and a time and resource budget. The agent can read and modify the cloned repo. It cannot touch production infrastructure, access secrets outside its scope, or persist state between invocations. We run these sandboxes on Modal. The cold start overhead is acceptable (a few seconds), and the isolation guarantees are strong. The alternative — running agents on shared infrastructure with permission scoping — is fragile and eventually breaks. Context management is the entire game The quality of an agent's output is determined almost entirely by the quality of its context. A code review agent that only sees the diff will produce shallow, generic comments. A code review agent that sees the diff, the full files, the related test files, the style guide, the git history, and the PR description will produce reviews that read like they came from a senior engineer who knows the codebase. We spent more engineering time on context assembly than on any other component. The system that determines which files to include, how to chunk them, what metadata to attach, and how to order them within the prompt is the most important system in the stack. Key lessons on context: Retrieval matters more than generation. The model is good at reasoning over information it has. It is bad at reasoning about information it does not have. Getting the right files into context is more impactful than prompt engineering. Static analysis is underrated. Language servers, AST parsing, import graph traversal — these tools are old, boring, and extremely useful for determining which files are relevant to a given change. Context windows are large but not infinite. Even with 200k-token context windows, you cannot include an entire monorepo. Prioritization and truncation strategies matter. We rank files by relevance and include them in priority order until the budget is exhausted. Cost control requires architecture, not just optimization LLM API calls are expensive. A naive implementation — send the entire repo context on every invocation — will produce accurate results and astronomical bills. Cost control is an architectural concern, not an optimization pass. We use three strategies: Tiered model selection. Not every task needs the most capable model. Routing simple tasks (formatting checks, style lint) to faster, cheaper models and complex tasks (architectural review, bug detection) to more capable models reduces cost by 60-70% with negligible quality impact. Incremental processing. When a PR is updated, we do not re-review the entire PR. We identify which files changed since the last review and only re-process those files. This reduces token usage by 40-50% on iterative PRs. Caching and deduplication. Repository metadata, style guides, and common file contents are cached across invocations. The same file does not get re-tokenized on every review. Reliability is about retries, not accuracy LLM outputs are non-deterministic. The same input will sometimes produce a great review and sometimes produce a mediocre one. You cannot fix this by making the model more accurate. You fix it by building reliability at the system level. Our approach: every agent invocation goes through a structured output pipeline. The agent produces structured JSON (not free-form text). A validation layer checks the output against a schema. If the output is malformed or incomplete, the system retries with a corrective prompt. If it fails after three attempts, it falls back to a simpler analysis. In production, the first attempt succeeds about 92% of the time. After retries, the success rate is 99.7%. The remaining 0.3% falls back gracefully — the user gets a partial result or a notification that the agent could not complete the task, rather than a broken comment or a silent failure. Testing LLM agents is hard but possible You cannot write a unit test that asserts an LLM will produce a specific output. The output is non-deterministic and the quality is subjective. But you can build an evaluation framework that catches regressions. Our testing strategy has three layers: Deterministic tests for everything outside the LLM call — context assembly, output parsing, integration posting. These are standard unit and integration tests. Snapshot evaluations for agent output quality. We maintain a corpus of 200+ test cases — real PRs with known issues — and run the agent against them on every deploy. We measure recall (did the agent find the known issues?) and precision (did it flag things that are not issues?). Production monitoring for real-world quality. We track which agent comments get resolved (accepted as useful) vs. dismissed. This gives us a continuous quality signal from actual users. The things that actually matter After fifteen months, here is what we believe matters most for production LLM agents: Context quality. What information the model has access to determines the ceiling for output quality. No amount of prompt engineering overcomes missing context. Structured output. Free-form text output is unparseable and unreliable. Structured JSON with schema validation and retry logic is the baseline for production systems. Isolation. Autonomous agents that can execute code must be sandboxed. There is no middle ground. Configurability. Users need to control what the agent does, when it runs, and what it flags. Default behavior will never be right for everyone. Cost architecture. Design for cost from day one. Model routing, incremental processing, and caching are not optimizations — they are requirements. The models will keep getting better. The infrastructure around them — context, reliability, cost, safety — is what determines whether an agent is a demo or a production system.

title: Collaborative Trial: On Optimizing Recommendation Testing
summary: Taboola is responsible for billions of daily recommendations, and we are doing everything we can to make those recommendations fit each viewer’s personal taste and interests. We do so by updating our Deep-Learning based models, increasing our computational resources, improving our exploration techniques and many more. All those things though, have one thing in common […]
body_text: Taboola is responsible for billions of daily recommendations, and we are doing everything we can to make those recommendations fit each viewer’s personal taste and interests. We do so by updating our Deep-Learning based models, increasing our computational resources, improving our exploration techniques and many more. All those things though, have one thing in common – we need to understand if a change is for the better or not, and we need to do so while allowing many tests to run in parallel. We can think of many KPI’s for new algorithmic modifications – system latency, diversity of recommendations or user-interaction to name a few – but at the end of the day, the one metric that matters most for us in Taboola is RPM (revenue per mill, or revenue per 1,000 recommendations), which indicates how much money and value we create for our customers on both sides – the publishers and advertisers. RPM can get a little noisy – it is influenced by external factors such as current events (how interesting the news is right now) or time of year (aren’t we all waiting for the holidays?) but also by internal factors such as system upgrades and our own experiments – which can affect one another and add extra noise to the mix. All those mean that RPM can change by as much as 5-10% from day to day. But an algorithmic improvement, on the other hand, might be even lower than 1%. So how can we tell if a change is for the better? All it takes is proper data handling and some pretty basic statistics. The Simpsons Let’s start with data handling. With the enormous amount of data we handle at Taboola, you can rest assured that we’ve seen many interesting phenomena that caused us to scratch our heads. For instance, take a look at the data in the table below, which shows how well two variants are doing on a four day period. If you look carefully you’ll see that in each of the 4 days, the test variant has higher RPM values than the default variant. However, when aggregating results from all 4 days the default variant all of the sudden has a higher RPM. This brings up two questions: How is that possible? Is the test variant winning or losing? default variant test variant date RPM count revenue RPM count revenue 2020-05-01 1.358 123,651,344 167,896 1.399 41,385,732 57,888 2020-05-02 1.190 157,182,560 186,992 1.200 77,811,946 93,370 2020-05-03 1.068 151,712,429 161,976 1.075 74,929,584 80,538 2020-05-04 0.988 141,997,417 140,288 0.995 70,248,390 69,864 Grand Total 1.144 574,543,750 657,152 1.141 264,375,652 301,661 Table 1: Daily stats for two variants over the course of 4 days First off, this is not only possible, but can actually happen quite often. This phenomenon is called “Simpson’s paradox”, where combining several groups together cancels out a trend that appears individually in each group (you can read more on Simpson’s Paradox here ). The answer to the second question is hidden in the first day – take a close look at the second table below, which presents the traffic counts for each variant and the ratio between them: date default count test count count ratio 2020-05-01 123,651,344 41,385,732 0.33 2020-05-02 157,182,560 77,811,946 0.50 2020-05-03 151,712,429 74,929,584 0.49 2020-05-04 141,997,417 70,248,390 0.49 Grand Total 574,543,750 264,375,652 0.46 Table 2: Comparing the number of recommendations each variant had It can be seen that in the first day of the experiment, the ratio is way off (0.33 compared to 0.49-0.5 on other days). Looking closely into the matter we found out that we included the day of the variant setup in the experiment, so it was a full day for the default variant and a partial day for the test variant. Because the first day happened to be the most profitable day by far (check out the RPM columns in the first table), and because the test variant got a smaller chunk of it, its overall measure was lower even though it had better measures on all 4 days. What we learn from this example is that taking a look at the traffic split between variants, and making sure it is consistent, is important if we wish to avoid strange skews in the data. Our testing procedure in Taboola tests for such cases and others, and gives the researcher a green light if the experiment is winning with confidence, a red light if it is losing with confidence and an alert if some issues were found that need a closer look. It’s T-Time And how exactly do we gain this confidence? This brings us to the statistical part of this blogpost, or more specifically, to a paired sample t-test. Paired sample t-test is used when we can match each observation from one sample to an observation from the other. For our case we use the daily average revenue as a single data point, and the pairing is done over days. This means that for each variant we have a sequence of numbers and just like a normal t-test, we try to reject the null hypothesis: : The means of the test variant RPM and default variant RPM are equal But while a normal t-test goes like this: ( and are the unbiased estimators for the sample mean and sample variance respectively) A paired sample t-test goes like this: The great advantage of the paired sample t-test over the normal t-test is that it allows us to cancel the time related noise and focus on the difference between the two variants. For example, take a look at the results given in the following figure: Figure 1: Left: average revenue (per recommendation) of two variants over the course of 21 days Right: the difference in the average revenue along the same 21 days Using the normal t-test to compare the two variants, we get a p-value of ~0.7, which means we have about 30% confidence in rejecting the null hypothesis that the two variants have equally distributed means. This happens because the difference between days is much greater than the average difference between test and default. However, using the paired sample t-test yields a p-value of ~0.001, or 99.9% confidence in rejecting our null hypothesis (I will not dive into the subtleties of the confidence term, let’s keep it simple). If you need more intuition as to why the paired sample t-test improves the confidence to such an extent, compare the figure above to the one below – which shows a permutation of the days for test and default data such that we can no longer pair by days. In a sense, the un-paired t-test uses the data representation below while the paired t-test uses the data representation above. Figure 2: Same test and default variants, but this time days are permuted randomly so that pairing is not known Whenever using a statistical test, it is important to ask ourselves if it’s the right one. In our case, we made sure our data meets these 3 requirements for using a t-test: The sample means for both populations are normally distributed. For large samples this assumption is met due to the central limit theorem, but for smaller samples this needs to be tested. We use daily aggregated data so our sample is as big as the amount of days in the experiment, which is typically not very large. To test this requirement, we used the Shapiro-Wilk normality test and got good results. The two samples have the same variance. This is only required when the samples are not of equal size. We have equal size samples, and t-test is very robust to cases with unequal variance, so no worries there. The sampling should either be entirely independent or entirely paired. Our daily data is linked through the general behavior on each day, which means we need to perform a paired test, and that is exactly what we did. Final Words When we are testing new variants of our system we face contradicting interests. On the one hand, we want to make decisions fast – removing losing variants quickly and diverting more traffic to the winning ones yields greater value. On the other hand, the more time we give our variants, the more certainty we have in their performance, reducing the chance of making wrong decisions. This post gives a peek at how we use some pretty basic statistical principles and combine them with general “know-hows” of data handling in order to balance those interests, and make sure we gain as much information as possible from the time we give our variants. Have any thoughts? Let us know!

title: Google's Gemini AI Revolutionizes Spreadsheets with Auto Charts
summary: Google introduces Gemini AI for Google Sheets, a groundbreaking feature that transforms spreadsheet data into insightful charts automatically. body_text: Sheet Savvy: Automatic Data Visualizations Google's Gemini AI Revolutionizes Spreadsheets with Auto Charts Google introduces Gemini AI for Google Sheets, a groundbreaking feature that transforms spreadsheet data into insightful charts automatically. By generating Python code or using formulas, Gemini offers static image outputs that enhance your data storytelling. Available on most Workspace plans by February 2025, this new tool is set to democratize data visualization—but watch out for its static nature, requiring manual updates for new data. Introduction to Gemini AI in Google Sheets Gemini AI represents a significant advancement in how data can be interpreted and visualized using Google Sheets. By automatically generating charts and visual representations through AI‑driven technology, users can realize time savings and increased productivity. This feature is particularly valuable to those without technical expertise in coding, democratizing access to complex data insights. The new feature leverages the capabilities of Python and spreadsheet formulas to transform static data into visual formats. While this capability emphasizes ease of use, it also introduces new considerations regarding data integrity and the accuracy of AI‑generated visual patterns. These enhancements are accessible under most Google Workspace plans and for Google One AI Premium subscribers, representing a major adoption effort by Google. Despite the promising aspects of this technology, some concerns remain, primarily regarding its limitations such as the creation of static images which do not update automatically with changing data. Users must remain aware of potential performance impacts arising from inconsistent data formatting and the limitations of current AI‑driven outputs. Interestingly, while the general response from the public has been positive, driven by the aspiration for more efficient workflows and retained simplicity, the expert opinions suggest careful handling of the tool to maximize its utility without overstretching its current capabilities. This suggests an ongoing dialogue between what AI can currently achieve and what users expect in dynamic data environments. Moving forward, Gemini AI's impact signals broader implications across economic, social, and regulatory aspects, with potential cost savings and onboarding of new professional roles in data visualization. These changes are set within a rapidly evolving landscape of competition and regulatory frameworks, pushing for transparency and more refined AI solutions. As these tools continue to develop, both the opportunities and challenges for smarter, real‑time data interaction remain points of active exploration and innovation. Features and Capabilities of Gemini AI Gemini AI, an innovative feature introduced by Google for Google Sheets, showcases a significant advancement in automating data visualization from spreadsheet data. This technology leverages its capability to write Python code or utilize spreadsheet formulas, enabling it to convert data into static chart images. As part of its strategic rollout, the feature is accessible to most Google Workspace plans and Google One AI Premium subscribers, with a complete rollout planned by February 20th, 2025. This accessibility reflects Google's commitment to enhancing user experience through advanced AI tools. The chart generation process with Gemini AI involves an intelligent analysis of spreadsheet data to generate the corresponding Python code or spreadsheet formulas. This process facilitates the creation of appropriate visualizations, thereby simplifying complex data transformation tasks. However, a notable limitation is that the resulting charts are static, necessitating manual regeneration upon any change in the underlying data. Additionally, the tool's performance can be hindered by inconsistent data formatting and vague user prompts, highlighting areas where further refinement is needed. How Gemini AI Generates Visualizations Google's Gemini AI introduces an innovative way to automate data visualization directly within Google Sheets. Specifically designed to facilitate easier access to complex data insights, Gemini AI interprets spreadsheet data to output visual representations like charts, either by auto‑generating Python scripts or enhancing spreadsheet formulas. The capability aims to assist a broad audience, as it becomes available to most Google Workspace users and Google One AI Premium subscribers. However, it's crucial to recognize that the generated charts are currently static images. This characteristic implies that any changes to the underlying data necessitate a manual chart regeneration, a limitation that might affect processes needing real‑time updates. Gemini's integration highlights a step towards democratizing data visualization, as noted by experts like Sarah Chen from Deloitte, who points out that such tools lower the entry barriers for non‑technical users engaging in data analysis. On the flip side, librarians of these automation capabilities underline the restrictions inherent in static visualization outputs. The reactions from the public, gathered across various social media and professional platforms, underscore divided opinions. While many laud the potential time‑saving and productivity benefits, others express skepticism over its readiness for more complex, research‑oriented tasks. Concerns predominantly revolve around its static nature and potential inaccuracy when faced with inconsistent data inputs. Limitations and Challenges of Using Gemini AI Gemini AI's integration into Google Sheets represents a significant leap towards democratizing data visualization, enabling users, regardless of their technical prowess, to generate complex charts from raw spreadsheet data. However, like any burgeoning technology, Gemini AI is not without its constraints and potential obstacles. One primary limitation of the Gemini AI is its output format. Currently, the AI generates static image charts that do not automatically update when the source data changes. This necessitates manual intervention to refresh the visualization, undermining the purported efficiency in scenarios where data is frequently updated. This static nature could significantly hamper real‑time data analysis and decision‑making processes, driving a wedge in workflows that prioritize agility and speed. Moreover, the performance of Gemini AI can be inconsistent, heavily relying on the quality and formatting of the input data. If data is not formatted correctly or is inconsistent, the AI‑generated charts may not accurately represent the intended insights, potentially leading to misunderstandings and incorrect business decisions. Furthermore, the tool's dependency on precise and clear user prompts can be problematic in hectic or multi‑tasking environments where ambiguity might creep into instructions, affecting the accuracy of the outputs. Access to this AI‑driven feature is another notable challenge. While Gemini AI is available to multiple Google Workspace plans and Google One AI Premium subscribers, there are vague exclusions to certain plans, which might restrict access to a broader user base eager to embrace this technology. Additionally, the inclusion of Gemini in recent Workspace plan price hikes may pose a barrier to smaller organizations or individuals operating under tight budget constraints. Beyond the immediate technical and access issues, the broader implications and user expectations pose challenges as well. As users grow accustomed to AI‑facilitated analytics, there may be an exaggerated reliance on these tools without a foundational understanding of data principles. This could lead to a potential skill gap and misinterpretations of the AI outputs if users take the AI conclusions at face value without question. The emerging competitive landscape also adds a degree of pressure and difficulty. As major firms like Microsoft and Meta develop parallel services, Google will need to not only innovate continually but also keep costs competitive to maintain market share. Nonetheless, the regulatory landscape shaped by laws like the EU's AI Act adds another layer of complexity, requiring compliance and potentially influencing the design and availability of future AI features. In conclusion, while Gemini AI for Google Sheets highlights a transformative step forward in data visualization, several limitations and challenges require attention. Ensuring real‑time adaptability, improving accessibility, maintaining a balance of quality, and navigating both competitive and regulatory terrains are crucial to fully realizing Gemini AI's potential and user satisfaction. Accessibility and Cost Implications The integration of Gemini AI into Google Sheets introduces notable accessibility advantages, reducing the barrier to entry for data visualization. Users lacking technical expertise can benefit from AI‑driven insights without needing to write code or complex formulas. This democratization of technology can broaden access to advanced data analysis tools, particularly for smaller businesses or individuals without dedicated data teams. However, accessibility benefits come with associated costs, both direct and indirect. While this feature is rolled out to most Google Workspace plans, recent price increases suggest a financial commitment that may not be feasible for all potential users. Furthermore, organizational investment is required to ensure data quality and proper formatting, crucial for generating meaningful visualizations. From a broader perspective, the cost implications extend beyond mere financial outlay. The automation of routine data tasks could lead to workforce restructuring, as demand for traditional data visualization roles could decrease. It is critical for companies to strategically plan employee training and development to focus on AI‑assisted data analysis capabilities, aligning workforce skills with technological advancements. Additionally, the indirect costs linked with possible over‑reliance on AI‑generated outputs must be considered. Users might overlook data intricacies or become complacent, trusting AI‑generated insights without adequate validation. This highlights the necessity for a balanced approach, where human oversight complements AI efficiency, ensuring data interpretations are both accurate and contextually relevant. In summary, while Google's Gemini AI introduces exciting opportunities for enhanced data accessibility and potential cost savings, companies must weigh these benefits against the associated costs and adapt proactively to harness these innovations responsibly. Rollout Timeline and Availability The rollout timeline for Google's new Gemini AI feature in Google Sheets is set to be fully deployed by February 20th, 2025. This feature will become available to most Google Workspace users and Google One AI Premium subscribers during this period. Despite promising functionality, adoption will be gradual, taking into account the diverse user base relying on Google Sheets worldwide. In terms of availability, the feature is designed to integrate seamlessly into existing Google Sheets infrastructures without immediate additional costs on its own, although its inclusion comes with the recently updated Workspace Business plan pricing. Most users under various Google Workspace plans will have access, though specifics regarding excluded tiers have not been fully disclosed. During its rollout phase, Gemini AI's reach will align with pre‑existing account setups for ease of integration, minimizing the need for user adjustments. As the deployment progresses, feedback will likely guide necessary adjustments to improve functionality, efficiency, and user experience, ensuring that the tool not only adapts to different business needs but also conforms to regional compliance frameworks such as the EU's AI Act. Industry Context and Related Developments The AI landscape is vast and continually evolving, with significant developments across major technology companies highlighting the industry's trajectory. One notable advancement is Google's introduction of the Gemini AI feature for Google Sheets, revolutionizing how users generate data visualizations from spreadsheets. By automating the process through Python code or spreadsheet formulas, Gemini simplifies the creation of static image outputs, providing a significant tool for Google Workspace users and Google One AI Premium subscribers. This innovation in data visualization is among several key trends in AI deployment and development. OpenAI's launch of GPT‑5, which boasts enhanced multimodal capabilities, presents a competitive challenge to Google's Gemini 2.0, particularly in enterprise solutions aiming to streamline automation and analytics processes. Concurrently, Microsoft has integrated advanced AI agents throughout its Office 365 suite, focusing on autonomous document processing and meeting support - features akin to what Google is pursuing with its Workspace AI implementations. Meanwhile, Meta has unveiled Llama 3, an open‑source AI model that rivals Gemini in performance benchmarks, underscoring the competitive dynamics of AI development within the enterprise sector. The enforcement of the EU's AI Act has also added complexity to the market, prompting companies like Google to refine their AI strategies to comply with new regulations while continuing to roll out their offerings across geographical markets. These developments illustrate a clear shift towards more sophisticated and integrated AI solutions, as companies navigate regulatory landscapes and strive to address both competitive pressures and consumer expectations. The increasing capabilities and broader adoption of AI tools are set to reshape industry practice, impacting everything from routine data analysis tasks to high‑level strategic decision‑making in businesses worldwide. Expert Opinions on Gemini AI The launch of Gemini AI by Google Sheets represents a fusion of AI capabilities with traditional spreadsheet applications, introducing a tool that enables users to create data visualizations effortlessly. However, this innovation is met with both enthusiasm and scrutiny. Tech experts highlight its democratizing potential in data analytics while pointing out that static image outputs require frequent manual updates, hindering seamless user experience. Data analytics expert Sarah Chen lauds the feature as a groundbreaking move towards making data visualization accessible to non‑technical users, echoing sentiments elsewhere in the industry about its significant impact on how businesses manage data. Dr. Michael Thompson also emphasizes the potential efficiencies while highlighting the challenges of ensuring data quality. Despite its promise, tech analyst Maria Rodriguez articulates that Gemini AI currently meets basic visualization needs but falls short on more complex analysis demands. Meanwhile, David Park, a business intelligence consultant, highlights potential workflow constraints due to the need for chart regeneration. In public discourse, Gemini AI receives a mix of excitement and skepticism. While the platform's potential to save time and enhance workflow is appreciated, concerns remain about its reliability for complex data management. The tool's limited availability is also a point of contention for users eager to integrate it into their routine operations. Looking ahead, the integration of AI into common tools like Google Sheets may redefine business data strategies. The transformative potential lies not just in cost and time efficiencies, but also in the broader implications for the skill sets required in data analysis roles. Moreover, as regulatory environments like the EU AI Act influence deployment, the evolution of AI technologies must account for compliance and ethical considerations. Technologically, the future trajectory of tools like Gemini AI will likely shift towards real‑time data visualization and predictive analytics. Competition among AI solutions promises a rapid advancement in capabilities, ensuring that businesses can adapt to an increasingly data‑driven landscape. Public Reception and Feedback The public reception of Google's Gemini AI feature for Google Sheets has been met with a blend of optimism and skepticism. Social media platforms such as Reddit have users expressing enthusiasm about the potential for democratizing data visualization, which is particularly beneficial for those without coding expertise. Many users are excited about the promising time‑saving features and the potential for streamlined workflows that this AI tool can offer. Despite the excitement, there is a healthy amount of skepticism, especially from tech‑savvy forums and communities. A notable concern is Gemini's reliability. Critics argue that the tool can be unreliable, especially for research purposes, due to its limitations. Technical discussions highlight the risk of oversimplification of complex data management issues, urging users to be cautious. Among the specific criticisms are the static nature of the image outputs which require manual rerunning for updates, and the limited availability of the feature across different Google Workspace plans. Some users find this exclusivity frustrating. Another significant worry is the potential for errors when dealing with inconsistent or incomplete data, which could lead to inaccurate visualizations. Furthermore, there is apprehension about the potential misinterpretation of AI‑generated charts by users who may not be familiar with data analytics, raising questions about the appropriate use and reliance on such tools. Overall, while there is cautious optimism about the benefits of Gemini AI, there is also an acknowledgment of its current limitations, with hopes for future improvements. Future Developments and Implications The launch of Google's Gemini AI feature in Google Sheets marks a significant technological advancement in data analysis automation. As it stands, companies adopting this technology can expect substantial time savings in routine analytic tasks, potentially enhancing productivity and providing a competitive edge. There's a growing need for transparent AI operations, especially in industries governed by strict regulations, prompting businesses to develop new standards for AI applications in analytics. title: Postgres: View vs Materialized View - Choosing the Right One
summary: Postgres offers two distinct types of views: standard views and materialized views. Standard views operate as virtual tables that reflect real-time data.
body_text: Postgres offers two distinct types of views: standard views and materialized views. Standard views operate as virtual tables that reflect real-time data, whereas materialized views store query results physically and need periodic refreshes. This distinction is crucial for optimizing database performance and ensuring data integrity. It’s essential to choose the right type of view based on your specific requirements for data freshness and query performance. Let’s explore these considerations in detail, aiding in choosing the optimal view type for your specific needs. What are standard views in PostgreSQL? In Postgres, a standard view acts as a virtual table, directly reflecting the latest data. This ensures that every query against the view executes the underlying SQL statement in real time, simplifying complex queries and maintaining data consistency. Here’s how you can create a standard view: CREATE VIEW example_view AS SELECT column1, column2 FROM some_table WHERE condition = true; Choose standard views for scenarios requiring up-to-the-minute data without significantly impacting database performance. What are materialized views in PostgreSQL? Unlike standard views, materialized views in Postgres cache the query result as a physical table. This caching significantly speeds up query times for complex operations since the database doesn’t need to re-execute the original SQL query with each access. However, remember to refresh the view to update its data: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW example_materialized_view AS SELECT column1, column2 FROM some_table WHERE condition = true; To refresh this materialized view, use the following command: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW example_materialized_view; Materialized views are ideal for complex, data-heavy queries where it’s acceptable for the information to be slightly outdated. Choosing between standard and materialized views Your choice between standard and materialized views should align with your data access needs and query performance requirements: Opt for standard views when you need immediate access to the most current data. Choose materialized views for complex queries where improved performance outweighs the need for the latest data. Making the correct choice between these two view types can significantly enhance your Postgres database’s efficiency and effectiveness.

title: How to Create a Materialized View in MySQL
summary: A materialized view is a database object that contains the results of a query. It’s similar to a regular view, except that the data is physically stored.
body_text: A materialized view is a database object that contains the results of a query. It’s similar to a regular view, except that the data is physically stored. This is good because it makes it faster to retrieve data, which helps for stuff like complex queries. This guide walks you through how to create one in MySQL. What is a materialized view? Full disclosure: MySQL doesn’t natively support materialized views. However, you can simulate one using a combination of a regular view and a physical table. You have to create a table to store the query result and then periodically refresh that table to keep the data up to date. Create a base table and view Step 1: Create a base table Start by creating a base table that will store the materialized data. This table’s structure should match the result of the query you intend to materialize. CREATE TABLE materialized_view_table ( -- Define columns here ); Step 2: Create a view Next, create a view that defines the query you want to materialize. CREATE VIEW my_view AS SELECT -- Define your query here ; Populate the materialized view Refresh the materialized view Since MySQL doesn’t automatically refresh materialized views, you need to implement a mechanism to periodically update the base table with the latest data. TRUNCATE TABLE materialized_view_table; INSERT INTO materialized_view_table SELECT * FROM my_view; You can automate this process using events or triggers. Query the materialized view To retrieve data, simply query the base table. SELECT * FROM materialized_view_table; The advantage of this approach is that it’s faster to retrieve data than if you just queried the view directly. Managing updates To keep the materialized view up-to-date, consider implementing a scheduled job that runs the refresh query at regular intervals. You can do this with MySQL events or external schedulers. title: Migrate Apollo Federation 1.0 Supergraphs to Apollo Federation 2.0
body_text: We’re announcing an important update: starting with the 1.60 release of Apollo GraphOS Router and Apollo Router Core coming in the next few weeks, Apollo Federation 1.0 supergraphs will no longer be supported. This update accompanies the introduction of a new native query planner in these Apollo Router versions, marking a significant advancement in our technology. Upgrading to Apollo Federation 2.0 is essential to leverage these improvements fully, and as Federation and Apollo Router are mission-critical infrastructure for your API workloads, we are here to guide you through every step of this transition to confidently operating your GraphQL platform. Understanding the importance of upgrading The next Apollo Router versions, 1.60 and beyond, include a new native query planner with significant performance enhancements. Our extensive testing of over 620 million operations showed a median 10x improvement in query planning time, a 2.9x reduction in CPU utilization, and a 2.2x reduction in memory consumption. Designed specifically for Federation 2.0 supergraphs, this new query planner simplifies maintenance and enhances security by eliminating dependencies, including the need for a JavaScript execution engine within the Apollo Router process. Timeline and planning Federation 1.0 supergraphs have been marked as deprecated in our GraphOS Studio UI and users have not been able to create them since Q3 2023. With the upcoming new Apollo Router versions, support for Federation 1.0 supergraphs will end across all Apollo products, including Apollo Gateway. We strongly recommend you upgrade to Apollo Router and Federation 2.0 to ensure continued compatibility with our latest innovations. If you are still operating your GraphQL deployment without having yet migrated to Federation 2.0, upgrading to the new query planner in Apollo Router 1.60 and beyond will introduce a breaking change. Migration to Federation 2.0 is simple and focuses on the composition layer, without requiring changes to existing subgraphs in most cases. You only need to compose a supergraph with Federation 2.0 and typically your subgraphs can continue using Federation 1.0 until they need 2.0 features. Our migration guide details how you can update just your Federation composition step to compile a compatible supergraph. Available resources and ongoing support We recognize that transitioning from Federation 1.0 to Federation 2.0 is a significant step for some of our users. This decision reflects our commitment to eliminating the complexities of outdated technology and ensuring our offerings meet the evolving needs of modern API infrastructures. We are dedicated to transparent communication and improving our deprecation processes to help maintain the robustness, efficiency, and security of your systems. Apollo values your partnership and trust as we continue to innovate. We are here to support you through this transition to keep your API infrastructure powerful and future-proof. For additional support, please visit our Apollo Community or, for GraphOS users, contact our Technical Support team at support@apollographql.com . Written by Josh Lambert Read more by Josh Lambert

title: Popular Cities for Cybersecurity Jobs in 2026
summary: Cybersecurity is an attractive career for many reasons, including the number of cities with opportunities for cybersecurity professionals. Learn more about job roles to consider and the best cities for cybersecurity jobs across the country.
body_text: An increasing amount of information is stored on digital devices in industries ranging from e-commerce to health care to credit card services. With the rising incidence of data breaches , protecting that information is paramount. You can take part in building and maintaining security systems with a career in cybersecurity . Cybersecurity is a growing field; revenue in the industry is likely to grow 10.56 percent per year, reaching $273.6 billion worldwide by 2028 [ 1 ]. Read on to discover some of the best cities for cybersecurity jobs and the types of jobs that may be available. What is cybersecurity? Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting networks, devices, and data to prevent access by individuals who should not have it. This practice ensures the confidentiality, validity, and availability of information. In many people’s daily lives, technology is ever-present. This is the case, too, with organizations. Businesses often hold sensitive information that they are required by law to protect. Globally, the average cost of a data breach for a company reached $4.88M in 2024, a 10% increase year over year and the highest total ever, according to IBM [ 2 ]. Common cybersecurity attacks include: Malware P hishing Man-in-the-middle S tructured Query Language (SQL) injection Zero-day exploits Denial-of-service attacks, or DNS tunneling attacks Each of these attacks involves attackers infiltrating a network, gaining unauthorized access to a two-party transaction, or preventing a system from working properly. Enterprises such as credit card companies, health care organizations, e-commerce companies, and many more rely on robust cybersecurity departments to protect information. How much do data breaches cost organizations? The average data breach costs an organization $4.45 million, according to a 2023 report by IBM. That figure represents a 15 percent increase over three years [ 2 ]. Read more: 10 Common Types of Cyberattacks and How to Prevent Them Types of cybersecurity jobs Cybersecurity professionals typically specialize in different functions, including building security systems, testing defense mechanisms, and responding to attacks. The scope of your work may include developing emergency response plans, processing and analyzing data, and testing systems to ensure they are compliant with laws and industry regulations. The following list shows common cybersecurity job titles and their associated average salaries according to Glassdoor: Information security analyst: $113,878 [ 3 ] Digital forensic analyst: $76,783 [ 4 ] IT security auditor: $91,730 [ 5 ] Security systems administrator: $88,523 [ 6 ] Security engineer : $138,207 [ 7 ] Cryptography engineer: $138,382 [ 8 ] Cybersecurity manager: $153,216 [ 9 ] Security architect: $165,525 [ 10 ] Penetration tester: $114,003 [ 11 ] What are the best cities for cybersecurity jobs? Cybersecurity is a growing profession with career opportunities available in cities across the US. Whether you’d like to work in a booming metropolis or a small to midsize community, cybersecurity could offer opportunities in your preferred area. Explore some popular cities for cybersecurity jobs below, according to Glassdoor and BLS data, as well as an AdvisorSmith report that ranked 181 US cities based on average annual salary, location quotient, cost of living, and size, and CompTIA's State of the Tech Workforce 2024 report. Small cities Idaho Falls, ID The second-largest city in Idaho outside of the Boise metro area has a lot to offer for cybersecurity professionals. Idaho Falls is a hub for commerce and health care in the eastern part of the state. Idaho National Laboratory and Eastern Idaho Regional Medical Center have headquarters in Idaho Falls, presenting opportunities for cybersecurity jobs. AdvisorSmith, a business information resource, named Idaho Falls among its top cities for cybersecurity careers [ 12 ]. Ithaca, NY Ithaca, New York, is a small city with affluent prospects for cybersecurity professionals. According to AdvisorSmith, Ithaca ranked seventh among top cities for cybersecurity jobs [ 12 ]. This city is home to Cornell University and Ithaca College, two schools with respected computer science programs. Medium cities Bloomington, IL Bloomington, a city about two hours from Chicago, is a hub for tech jobs. Companies such as State Farm Insurance and COUNTRY Financial are headquartered here, and 74.862 per 1,000 residents work in the tech sector [ 13 ]. AdvisorSmith selected Bloomington as the top overall city for IT security analysts [ 12 ]. Huntsville, AL Many companies (Invariant Corporation, Nippon Express, Torch Technologies, and more) call Huntsville home, opening opportunities for cybersecurity professionals. Additionally, the significant presence of military and government contractors in Huntsville makes it an ideal center for IT careers. Trenton, NJ New Jersey ranks number one in broadband connectivity and number two in fastest download speeds, according to CompTIA. A strong talent pool supports the cybersecurity industry in Trenton, with the prestigious Princeton University in the city and a high education level—42 percent of Trenton’s workforce holds a bachelor’s degree or higher [ 14 ]. Trenton’s tech workforce will grow by 223 jobs in 2024, CompTIA projects [ 17 ]. San Jose, CA San Jose is the largest city in Silicon Valley, and tech jobs are plentiful, with 141.7 tech workers per 1,000 employees [ 15 ]. Silicon Valley is one of the country's most important hubs of technology innovation and entrepreneurship. This epicenter for IT careers has remained one of the top five areas for tech jobs, thanks to the thousands of start-up companies that operate here. Boulder, CO Boulder has a median annual salary of $75,396 for IT jobs, and the city supports technology-focused companies [ 16 ]. More than 17,000 tech workers live in the area. Cisco, IBM, Fanatics, CA Technologies, and Teamsnap all chose to base their operations in Boulder. Austin, TX Austin is a growing city that's highly ranked for its cost of living and wages for tech workers. It's also home to a growing cybersecurity industry. Employers in Austin advertised more than 45,000 IT job postings in 2023, according to CompTIA [ 17 ]. IT jobs in Austin have a median salary of $81,925 yearly [ 18 ]. Large cities Colorado Springs, CO Colorado Springs is smaller than many other major tech hubs in the country, but with 53.56 tech employees per 1,000 workers, cybersecurity is among the top career options in the city [ 19 ]. While the western region of the US features some major cities for tech jobs, Colorado Springs is a midsize option that offers the possibility of high salary and career growth. Washington, DC The nation’s capital ranked second in total employment of tech professionals in 2024, behind only New York City, according to CompTIA [ 17 ]. Washington, DC, is home to many government agencies and technology companies, which employ 239,700 in total [ 20 ]. Albuquerque, NM Albuquerque is another smaller but high-powered city for tech careers. Albuquerque has 11,730 working in tech jobs [ 21 ]. New Mexico’s largest city is also an excellent place for diversity in technology. CompTIA ranks New Mexico in its first diversity index quartile [ 17 ]. Seattle, WA Some of the biggest companies in the world, including Amazon, Starbucks, and Microsoft, base their operations in Seattle. A great deal of Seattle’s workforce is in tech, with 82.64 employees per 1,000 working in this sector [ 22 ]. Another popular spot for tech careers lies nearby, with Olympia, Washington, employing 6,360 tech employees [ 23 ]. San Francisco, CA San Francisco, a major city near Silicon Valley, is one of the premier places for cybersecurity careers. Tech jobs in San Francisco have grown steadily each year, with a 3.8 percent increase in jobs from 2023 to 2024, according to CompTIA [ 17 ]. The median salary for tech workers in the area is $96,117 [ 24 ]. New York, NY Among the largest cities in the world, New York City offers a great deal of opportunities in cybersecurity. New York is at the top of CompTIA’s rankings for tech employment, with 594,191 technology jobs in the city [ 17 ]. Cybersecurity professionals can make attractive salaries in NYC, with the average tech worker earning around $94,829 annually [ 25 ]. How to begin your job search The beginning of a job search is an ideal time to reflect on your values and aspirations. Considering your career goals, skills, and experience can help you choose an area to look for a job in. Decide on your ideal location and type of industry. Finding the perfect city to call home involves a lot of thought and consideration. Each location you explore for a new job will include advantages and disadvantages. If you're planning to relocate for a cybersecurity job, keep the following factors in mind: Lifestyle: Consider the size and feel of the city. Do you crave the energy and variety of a bustling metropolis or the peace and quiet of a small town? Suburbs offer a middle ground. Climate: Do you prefer sunshine and warmth year-round or distinct seasons with cooler winters? Think about how the weather will affect your day-to-day life and outdoor hobbies. Activities and culture: What are you passionate about? Does the city offer museums, theaters, and events that align with your interests? Are there opportunities for hiking, biking, or exploring nature? Cost of living: Research housing costs, groceries, transportation, and taxes. Can you comfortably live on your expected income in this city? Commute: How important is a short commute? When considering different areas, factor in public transportation options, traffic patterns, and average commute times. Read more: What Is a Good Salary? Review your qualifications and skills. Information security analysts typically hold bachelor’s degrees in majors such as computer and information technology. A background in topics such as engineering or mathematics can be helpful in cybersecurity jobs. Consider earning a certification. Certifications can affirm your skills and provide an advantage when applying for cybersecurity jobs. You may consider certification to boost your chances for employment in cybersecurity or take a step toward specializing in a particular area of the profession. Security+ is a common certification that you can earn through CompTIA. It establishes baseline skills and can help an entry-level cybersecurity professional learn more about cybersecurity work. For more experienced professionals, the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) validates experience with managing cybersecurity systems. This translates to a wealth of career opportunities for those interested in cybersecurity around the country. If you’re interested in starting a career in cybersecurity, consider the Google Cybersecurity Professional Certificate on Coursera. title: Upcoming Evidently API Changes
summary: The Evidently API is evolving — and it’s getting better! We are updating the open-source Evidently API to make it simpler, more flexible, and easier to use. Explore the new features.
body_text: The Evidently API is evolving — and it’s getting better! Be among the first to explore the new features and improvements. What's happening? We are updating the Evidently API to make it simpler, more flexible, and easier to use. As we focus more on LLM-related evaluations , we’re also working to futureproof the library for these workflows. These changes affect both the open-source library and the way how you programmatically interact with Evidently Cloud. We invite everyone to try out the new API and share feedback to help us refine the experience! Starting today, you can access the updated API by importing it from evidently.future . Explore the updated documentation and examples to dive in. New to Evidently? Welcome! Start with the new Quickstart Guides tailored for LLM or ML use cases. Already a user? Be sure to read the “What Changed” section below to understand what’s changing and ensure a smooth transition. These changes are paving the way for the Evidently 1.0 release, where the new API will become the default. The current API will remain available for a while, giving you time to adapt. What changed? Here’s the breakdown of what’s new and improved. Metrics redesign The Metric object in Evidently used to be pretty complex. As the library evolved, Metrics grew organically and acted like widgets, bundling multiple calculations and visualizations together. Parsing Metric results, even for our own dashboards, was tricky because each one had its own unique JSON structure. Now, the Metrics are much simpler. Each one has a fixed structure, outputs a single computation result, and lets you specify the visualization type directly as a parameter. No need to worry about Presets: they are here to stay. You can still use pre-built templates that combine various Metrics for common evaluation scenarios. For instance, Data Drift Preset is still available under the same name. What’s better now? Custom Metrics . Creating your own Metrics is much easier and more intuitive. Your custom Metrics will automatically fit with the rest of the framework, allowing you to use them in Tests, track them on Dashboards, etc. Parsing Metric results. JSON outputs are now standardized. This greatly simplifies downstream processing. Segmented evaluations . The new “Group by” feature lets you compute Metrics for specific classes or labels. For example, you can analyze Data Drift for subgroups of users within your dataset. Other quality-of-life improvements are in the works, such as an option to rename “reference” and “current” datasets. Unified Reports and Tests Reports and Test Suites are now merged into a single object. If you’ve ever wondered whether to compute a Report or a Test Suite — wonder no more. You can now handle both at once. Each still has its distinct role: Reports give a visual overview of all computed Metrics, like distribution summaries and value statistics. Tests let you set and view pass/fail conditions, such as checking for missing data or verifying that all LLM responses in a dataset meet quality thresholds. What used to be a Test Suite is now an optional extension of Reports. If you choose it, both types of outputs will appear in different tabs of the same HTML file. This way, you don’t have to save two different files and switch between them. You can still use the auto-generated Test conditions or define them yourself. It’s also now possible to set up relative conditions — like checking if values fall within +/-10% (or 20, or 30…) from the reference. Dashboard overhaul If you’ve been using the Evidently Dashboard to organize Reports and track evaluation results over time, the latest updates improve this experience. Simpler API for Dashboard Panel setup . The dashboards-as-code feature used to be a bit tricky when it came to configuring monitoring Panels. Since now each Metric’s output is standardized, you no longer have to deal with complex paths to point to specific results for plotting. Custom Metrics support . The Evidently UI fully supports custom Metrics. Even if you implemented a custom render for your Metric using Plotly, you’ll now be able to see the stored Report when you save it to your workspace — whether self-hosted or cloud. That’s a big deal! Text descriptors redesign Text descriptors are row-level text evaluations — anything from basic checks like text length to LLM-driven evals, such as determining whether an output contradicts its source. With the increasing focus on LLM-related metrics, we’ve updated the text descriptors API to make it more logical and easier to use. Descriptor computation is now split into two steps: Compute Descriptors and add them to the source table with inputs and outputs. Aggregate the results or run conditional checks. This change is especially useful when you want to perform multiple Tests or aggregations (no need to recompute the results!) or simply get the dataset with scores without the Report. Share your feedback! We know these updates introduce some breaking changes — we don’t make them lightly! A lot of this comes directly from the feedback we’ve gotten from the users. We implement these updates to make the library more maintainable and pave the way for new features. Our goal is less confusion, less repetition, and more functionality — all in one place. Check out the documentation and examples today, and let us know what you think! If you get stuck or have questions, drop by our Discord — we’re here to help! We’d love to hear your feedback! 🚀
